ops.new_text:
The contributions of the study are these:
\begin{itemize}
\item BTTN, a survival network whose ECG evidence passes through per-block frequency and lead factors, with a separate linear clinical term that does not pass through those factors.
\item An incident-AF cohort in MIMIC-IV-ECG defined from ICD-coded hospital diagnoses with a 30-day blanking window, reported with its exclusion counts.
\item A comparison of one-year discrimination against a clinical model, a CNN and linear block-term tensor regression (BTTR) under one protocol, and the discrimination of BTTN at four horizons, read from the same cross-validated risks without refitting for each horizon.
\item The calibration, risk stratification and operating points of BTTN with the clinical term.
\item A beat-aligned, energy-normalised occlusion profile of the ECG term of BTTN.
\end{itemize}

ops.rationale: States how the horizon risks were produced (each patient's risk from the fold that held the patient out: mean log-risk of three networks trained on the other four folds, a Cox model fitted on the same folds) and that they were read at every horizon without refitting; all AUROCs unchanged.
ops.new_text: Each patient's risk in the survival design came from the fold in which that patient was held out. For the fused model and ECG-only BTTN, it was the mean log-risk of three networks trained on the other four folds. The clinical Cox model was fitted on the same four folds. These cross-validated risks were read at every horizon without refitting (Table~\ref{tab:horizons}). The fused model had an AUROC of 0.723 [0.701, 0.745] at 120 days, for onset in the 90 days after the blanking window, 31 to 120 days after the index ECG. Its AUROC was 0.727 [0.711, 0.743] at one year, 0.740 [0.727, 0.753] at two years and 0.745 [0.735, 0.755] at five years. The clinical Cox model had point estimates of 0.710, 0.711, 0.727 and 0.731, below those of the fused model at each horizon. ECG-only BTTN ranged from 0.658 to 0.676. The four horizons share the same risks and overlapping patients. They describe the behaviour of each model and are not independent replications. One reason for the lower one-year values of the survival design is its control group. At one year it includes patients who develop AF later, whereas the controls of the one-year design have no AF diagnosis.

ops.new_text: On ICD-coded hospital diagnoses linked to MIMIC-IV-ECG, a block-term tensor network with a separate clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its AUROC was 0.7776, against 0.7597 for a clinical model and 0.7350 for a CNN. Without refitting for each horizon, it kept its point estimates above those of the clinical model at horizons from 120 days to five years after the index ECG. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed closely in most risk deciles. The fused model also flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Its gain over the clinical model is small, and the one-year intervals overlap. The gain is consistent in direction within one health system, and no interval for the difference yet establishes it.

ops.new_text: For the design of ECG risk models, the results suggest that a clinical term kept outside the block-term factors adds to the discrimination of the ECG term. At one year, the fused model reached 0.7776 [0.7664, 0.7888] and the ECG term alone 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517]. These two intervals do not overlap, although the study reports no paired interval for this difference. The clinical comparator used here is narrower than a full clinical score, and the readout is descriptive. Validation outside one health system, a test of the factors on ICD-coded labels and a comparator that includes the PR interval are the next requirements before any clinical use.
